title: Which kitchen gets the swap?
allegory: Denoising versus noising is like swapping one cook between a good kitchen and a sabotaged one: send a good cook into the sabotaged kitchen and see if the dish is rescued (enough), or a sabotaged cook into the good kitchen and see if the dish is ruined (needed).

chapters.name: Two kitchens
chapters.note: '...John gave a drink to' → Mary. Swap the subject and it breaks.

cap.1: You have two versions of a sentence: one the model gets right, one tweaked so it gets it wrong. You can move one internal value between them. Which way?
cap.2: Activation patching copies one activation from one run into the other. Clean run, corrupted run: the direction you choose decides what the result means.
cap.3: Patching sets one node to its value under the other input and lets everything downstream recompute. Which run you perturb decides whether you measure sufficiency or necessity.

cap.1: Good cook into the bad kitchen: if the dish is rescued, that cook was enough. Bad cook into the good kitchen: if the dish is ruined, that cook was needed.
cap.2: Denoising: run corrupted, patch in one clean activation; recovery means it is sufficient. Noising: run clean, patch in one corrupted activation; damage means it is necessary.
cap.3: Denoising tests a component's sufficiency with the rest corrupted; noising tests its necessity with the rest clean. Different questions, so in general different component sets.

cap.1: Score every experiment on one ruler: 0 means the dish tastes like the sabotaged kitchen's, 1 means it tastes like the good kitchen's.
cap.2: Normalise the logit difference so the corrupted baseline reads 0 and the clean baseline reads 1. In denoising, a component that restores the answer reads near 1.
cap.3: Under noising the same helpful component reads near −1, since it moves the metric away from the clean baseline. Name metric functions by direction and never share one colour scale.

chapters.name: Backups and lifters
chapters.title: two cooks: what each test sees

cap.1: Backup cooks, either one enough: ruin one and the other covers, so noising misses them. Pot lifters, both needed: rescue one alone and it still fails.
cap.2: Redundant parts act like OR: noising one shows nothing, denoising either restores it. Parts that work jointly act like AND: denoising one shows nothing, noising either breaks it.
cap.3: This is why the directions return different head sets: denoising finds sufficient pieces and misses AND-parts; noising finds necessary pieces and misses redundant OR-parts.

chapters.name: The overstated claim

right.title: What it means
lines: MLP0 acts like an extended embedding

chapters.verdict: Necessary is not the same as 'part of this circuit'.

cap.1: Take out the cook who unpacks every delivery and every dish fails. That cook matters, but not to this recipe in particular.
cap.2: Knocking out MLP0 in GPT-2 small wrecks performance on virtually any task, because it acts like an extended embedding. Necessary, yes; evidence for your specific circuit, no.
cap.3: Necessity is the weaker inference because components are interdependent: generic infrastructure is necessary for everything. Reporting noising results as 'the circuit' is the classic overstatement.

cap.1: Say which kitchen got the swap. 'Enough to fix it' and 'needed to keep it' are different claims, and mixing them up is how patching results get oversold.
cap.2: In [1.4.1] you run both directions on IOI and get different head sets. Put the direction in the metric's name and in the plot title.
cap.3: Circuit claims feed decisions about which components to monitor, ablate or steer. Knowing whether your evidence shows sufficiency or necessity is part of understanding a model honestly.

caption.1: Choose how two cooks share the job. When each does a part, both tests agree. Make them backups, or make them lift together, and watch the tests disagree.
caption.2: Bars are normalised scores: recovery from patching one clean part into the corrupted run, damage from patching one corrupted part into the clean run. OR hides from noising; AND hides from denoising.
caption.3: Additive: sufficiency and necessity coincide. OR: each part sufficient, neither necessary. AND: each necessary, neither sufficient. Real circuits mix all three, hence different head sets.

where_else: Path patching and circuit discovery, where the direction decides which edges you keep
Ablation studies anywhere in ML: removing a part tests necessity, adding it alone tests sufficiency
Reliability engineering: redundant backups hide from single-failure tests, two-key systems fail any single removal

hamming.what: The two directions of activation patching: clean values into a corrupted run (denoising) or corrupted values into a clean run (noising).
hamming.when: Every time you run a patching experiment and write down what it showed.
hamming.why: Denoising tests sufficiency and noising tests necessity, and redundant or jointly-acting parts answer the two differently, so the direction decides the claim.

object.title: The patching tabletop
object.subtitle: A table whose corners are the runs: sabotaged, good, and the two single-cook swaps in between.

cap.1: A tabletop for two cooks. One corner is the sabotaged kitchen at height 0; the opposite corner is the good kitchen at height 1.
cap.2: x is how clean component A is, y how clean B is; height is the normalised metric. (0,0) is the corrupted run, (1,1) the clean run.
cap.3: A two-component toy: height is the normalised logit difference as a function of which components carry clean values.

cap.1: When the cooks share the work, the table is a flat ramp and each side corner sits halfway up. Both tests agree.
cap.2: Additive: denoising A reads 0.5 and noising A costs 0.5. The two directions tell the same story.
cap.3: For additive contributions sufficiency and necessity coincide: f(1,0) = 1 − f(0,1).

cap.1: Backup cooks: either one alone lifts the table to full height. Rescue works; ruin never shows.
cap.2: OR: denoising either component recovers 1.0; noising either costs nothing, because the other covers.
cap.3: Redundancy: f(1,0) = f(0,1) = 1, so noising reports neither component as necessary.

cap.1: Pot lifters: the table only rises at the good corner. Rescue with one cook fails; ruin with one is total.
cap.2: AND: denoising either component recovers nothing; noising either destroys the behaviour.
cap.3: Conjunction: f(1,0) = f(0,1) = 0, so single-component denoising reports neither as sufficient.

cap.1: From above, the side corners are the experiments. 'Only A clean' is rescue-by-A, and it is also ruin-by-B.
cap.2: With just two components, denoising A and noising B land on the same corner, read against different baselines.
cap.3: In a two-component system denoise(A) and noise(B) evaluate the same state; the direction only changes which baseline you measure from.

predict.q: Two heads are backups for each other. You noise each one alone. What do you see?
predict.why: Each covers for the other, so neither is necessary alone. Denoising either one would show it is sufficient.

predict.q: Your write-up says 'these heads are the circuit', but you only ran noising. What did you actually show?

options.t: That they are necessary, not that they are sufficient

predict.why: Noising measures necessity. Saying the heads do the task needs sufficiency, which is what denoising tests.

object.where: Any system tested by swapping parts: failover servers behave like OR, two-key launch systems like AND.
